Thiruvananthapuram (Malayalam pronunciation: [t̪iɾuʋənən̪d̪ɐˈbuɾəm] ⓘ tirr-ROO-və-nun-Tə-poor-əm), also known as Trivandrum, is the capital city of the Indian state of Kerala.[9][10] As of 2011, the Thiruvananthapuram Municipal Corporation had a population of 957,730 over an area of 214.86 km2,[11] making it the most populous city in Kerala.[12] The larger Thiruvananthapuram metropolitan area has over 1.7 million inhabitants within an area of 543 km2, making it the second-most populous metropolitan area in Kerala after Kochi.[13]. Thiruvananthapuram is one of the few cities in India that serves as a state capital and is also centre for heritage, maritime activities, information technology, research and development, space research, defence, automotive technology, and biosciences. It is also among the few cities in the world where both an international airport and an international seaport are located within the city in close proximity to the city centre.[14]

Located on the west coast of India near the extreme south of the mainland, Thiruvananthapuram is a port city located 10 nautical miles (19 km; 12 mi)[15] from a heavily trafficked east–west shipping channel. The city is home to India's first deep-water trans-shipment port, owned by the Vizhinjam International Seaport Ltd. Thiruvananthapuram under the Government of Kerala.[16] The city is characterised by its undulating terrain of low coastal hills.[17] Thiruvananthapuram is also known for its cultural heritage, being associated with the musical contributions of Swathi Thirunal Rama Varma and the artistic legacy of painter Raja Ravi Varma. Thiruvananthapuram has contributed to the development of Malayalam literature through individuals like Ulloor S. Parameswara Iyer, Kumaran Asan, C. V. Raman Pillai and Narayana Guru. The city is also known for Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple, known as the richest temple in the world.[18] The other temples includes the Sreevaraham temple, the Shreekanteswaram temple and the Attukal Bhagavathy temple.
The present regions that constitute Thiruvananthapuram were ruled by the Ays who were related to feudatories of the Chera dynasty.[19] In the 12th century, it was conquered by the Kingdom of Venad.[19] In the 18th century, the king Marthanda Varma expanded the territory, founded the princely state of Travancore and made Thiruvananthapuram its capital.[20] Travancore became the most dominant state in Kerala by defeating the powerful Zamorin of Calicut in the battle of Purakkad in 1755.[21] Following India's independence in 1947, Thiruvananthapuram became the capital of Travancore–Cochin state and remained so until the new Indian state of Kerala was formed in 1956.[22][23]

Thiruvananthapuram is a notable academic and research hub and home to the University of Kerala, APJ Abdul Kalam Technological University, the regional headquarters of Indira Gandhi National Open University, and many other schools and colleges. Thiruvananthapuram is also home to research centres such as the National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology, the Indian Space Research Organisation's Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, the Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology, the National Centre for Earth Science Studies and a campus of the Indian Institutes of Science Education and Research.[24] Thiruvananthapuram is where India's space programme began, with the headquarters of Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre located there. The city is home to media institutions like Toonz Animation India and Tata Elxsi Ltd, and also to Chitranjali Film Studio, one of the first film studios in Malayalam Cinema, and Kinfra Film and Video Park at Kazhakoottam, which is India's first infotainment industrial park.[25]
In 2012, Thiruvananthapuram was named the best Kerala city to live in, by a field survey conducted by The Times of India.[26] In 2013, the city was ranked the fifteenth best city to live in in India, in a survey conducted by India Today.[27] Thiruvananthapuram was ranked the best Indian city for two consecutive years, 2015 and 2016, according to the Annual Survey of India's City-Systems (ASICS) conducted by the Janaagraha Centre for Citizenship and Democracy.[28] The city was also selected as the best governed city in India in a survey conducted by Janaagraha Centre for citizenship and democracy in 2017.[29]
Etymologyedit

The city takes its name from the Malayalam word thiru-anantha-puram (തിരുവനന്തപുരം [t̪iɾuʋɐnɐn̪d̪ɐpuɾɐm] ⓘ), meaning "The City of Lord Anantha (means infinite, endless, or eternal)",[30] referring to the deity of the Sri Padmanabhaswamy Temple located in the city. Thiruvananthapuram is also known in literature, and popular reference as Ananthapuri, derived from the Sanskrit word Syanandurapuram, meaning "The City of Bliss" in Carnatic kirtanas composed by Swathi Thirunal, erstwhile Maharaja of Travancore.[31] The city was officially referred to as Trivandrum until 1991 (Trivandrum being the anglicised name of the town), when the government decided to reinstate the city's original name Thiruvananthapuram. Many Malayalees still refer to the city as Trivandrum, however.[32] The city was also called as Anandapatnam or Anandapatam in Tamil and Telugu, meaning "The City of Ananda" which has the same meaning as the original name. [citation needed]
Historyedit  
Main article: History of Thiruvananthapuram

Pre-historic periodedit

Thiruvananthapuram is a relatively modern region with trading traditions dating back to 1000 BCE.[33][34] It is believed that the ships of King Solomon landed in a port then called Ophir (now Poovar) in Thiruvananthapuram in 1036 BCE.[35][36] The city was the trading post for spices, sandalwood and ivory.[37] However, the ancient political and cultural history of the city was almost entirely independent from that of the rest of Kerala. [citation needed]
Ancient periodedit
The southern region of present-day Kerala state (The coastal belt between Thiruvananthapuram and Alappuzha) was under the Ay dynasty, which was more related to the Pandya dynasty of Madurai.[38][page needed] The early rulers of the city were the Ays. Vizhinjam, which is now a region in present-day Thiruvananthapuram, was the capital of the Ay dynasty.[39] Vizhinjam was an important port city from as early as the second century BC.[40][41] During the Ay dynasty's rule, Thiruvananthapuram witnessed many battles in which the Chola and Pandyan dynasties attempted to capture the port town.[42][43]
Middle Agesedit
After the death of king Vikramaditya Varaguna in 925 AD, the glory of the Ays departed and almost all their territories became part of the Chera dynasty.[44][19] During the tenth century, the Cholas attacked and sacked Vizhinjam and surrounding regions.[19] The port in Vizhinjam and the historic education centre of Kanthalloor Sala were also destroyed by Cholas during this period.[45][46] A branch of the Ay family, which had controlled the Padmanabhaswamy Temple, merged with the Kingdom of Venad in the 12th century.[19]
A map of Malabar Coast drawn by Homann Heirs in 1733. At that time, Travancore was only a small territory wedged between Kollam and Kanyakumari, as shown in the map (Present-day districts of Thiruvananthapuram and Kanyakumari only).  
Early Modern periodedit

Tourism is a significant economic sector.[127][128][129] The presence of natural attractions like beaches, backwaters, hills, and plantations and attractions like heritage, history, Ayurveda, medical tourism and knowledge centres attract many tourists.[130] The city experienced a surge of investment in the real estate, infrastructure and retail sectors in 2016–17.[131]
Port-based developmentedit
Thiruvananthapuram is a commercial port city with port-related infrastructure due to the presence of the Deepwater Container Transhipment port operated by the Vizhinjam International Seaport Ltd. Thiruvananthapuram.[132]
The port is located close to international shipping routes, approximately 10 to 12 nautical miles (19 to 22 km) from the busy Persian Gulf–Malacca shipping lane.[133] It has a natural depth of 18 to 20 metres (59 to 66 ft), enabling it to accommodate large container vessels.[134] The berths are designed to handle vessels of up to 24,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU).[135] Port-related development has been associated with increased activity in logistics, warehousing, shipping services and supporting infrastructure, trade and transport connectivity.[citation needed]
Trivandrum Outer Ring Roadedit

The proposed Trivandrum Outer Ring Road (ORR) (ORR), also known as the Outer Area Growth Corridor (OAGC), is a major infrastructure initiative aimed at supporting the long-term economic development of the city and its surrounding region. The corridor, extending approximately 78–80 km between Vizhinjam International Seaport Thiruvananthapuram and Navaikulam, is planned as a six-lane access-controlled highway with designated economic zones along its alignment. The TOAGC master plan envisages the development of multiple sector-specific clusters, including logistics, industrial development, information technology, healthcare, health tourism, general tourism, education, and commercial services, forming an integrated investment region around the capital area. Key nodes such as Vizhinjam, Kovalam, Vembayam, Mangalapuram, and Nedumangad have been identified for focused development, including a logistics hub at Vizhinjam and a health and tourism hub in the coastal belt. The project is also expected to strengthen connectivity between Vizhinjam International Seaport, the IT corridors, and the national highway network, thereby facilitating port-led industrial growth and regional economic expansion.[136][137][138]
Tourismedit  
Main article: Tourism in Thiruvananthapuram  
Harvesting lotus leaves from Vellayani Lake.
Thiruvananthapuram is a major tourist hub in India.[128] Kovalam and Varkala are popular beach towns near the city.[139] Other important beaches include Poovar, Shankumugham Beach, Azhimala Beach, Vizhinjam Beach and Veli Beach. Other places of interest include the Agasthyamala rain forests, Neyyar Wildlife Sanctuary, Kallar, Braemore, Ponmudi hills, Poovar, the Anchuthengu backwaters, Varkala Cliffs and Kappil-Edava lakes. [citation needed]
The city is also known for its unique style of architecture involving Kerala Architecture with British and Dravidian influences.[140] Napier museum, Thiruvanathapuram Zoo, Padmanabha Swamy temple, Kuthira Malika palace, Kilimanoor palace and The Thiruvananthapuram Golf Club heritage building are examples of this. [citation needed]

The main museums include the Kerala Science and Technology Museum (with its attached Priyadarsini Planetarium), the Napier Museum, the Kerala Soil Museum and the Koyikkal Palace Museum. Agasthyamala Biosphere Reserve is listed in UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves.[141]
Cultureedit  
Main article: Culture of Thiruvananthapuram  
Established in 1855, the Napier Museum contains a vast collection of Ancient paintings and archaeological artefacts
Thiruvananthapuram is known as the "Evergreen City of India" because of its green landscapes and the presence of many public parks.[142] Thiruvananthapuram has historically been a cultural hub in Southern India due to the development of arts, architecture and liberal customs by the rulers of erstwhile Thiruvananthapuram. As a testimony to this, renowned artists like Maharaja Swathi Thirunal and Raja Ravi Varma hail from the city.[143][144] Prominent social reformers such as Sri Narayana Guru, Chattampi Swamikal, Ayyankali, Vakkom Moulavi and C. V. Raman Pillai also are from Thiruvananthapuram.[145]

Two of the three Malayalam triumvirate poets, Ulloor S. Parameswara Iyer and Kumaran Asan are from Thiruvananthapuram.[146][147] Annual literature festivals like the Kovalam Literary Festival, are held in the city.[148] Literary development is further aided by state institutions such as the State Central Library, one of the oldest public libraries in India, which was established in 1829,[149] and other major libraries including the Thiruvananthapuram Corporation Central library, and the Kerala University Library.[150] Thiruvananthapuram has been a hub of classical music since the days of Maharaja of Travancore, Swathi Thirunal.[151][152] Thiruvananthapuram is known for many music festivals like the Navarathri Music Festival, one of the oldest festivals of its kind in South India,[151] Swathi Sangeethotsavam, Soorya Music fest, Neelakanta Sivan Music Fest and many other music festivals are organised by various cultural groups.[151] The 111-day-long Soorya Festival is the biggest art and cultural event in Kerala.[153][154] The Soorya Festival features film festivals, theatre festivals, dance, music, painting and photography exhibitions.[153]
16th IFFK 2011 banner at Kairali Theater Complex

The Malayalam film Industry was started in Thiruvananthapuram. The first Malayalam feature film, Vigathakumaran, directed by J. C. Daniel, was released in Thiruvananthapuram.[155] J. C. Daniel is considered the father of the Malayalam film industry. He also established the first film studio in Kerala, the Travancore National Pictures at Thiruvananthapuram in 1926.[156][157] The International Film Festival of Kerala (IFFK), which is held every year in December, is one of Asia's largest film festivals in terms of viewer participation.[158][159] In addition to various film festivals, the presence of the Central Board of Film Certification's regional office, many movie studios and production facilities like the Uma Studio, Chitranjali Studio, Merryland Studio, Kinfra Film and Video Park and Vismayas Max contribute to the growth of Thiruvananthapuram as a centre of cinema.[160][161]
Apart from the famous Padmanabhaswamy Temple, the city's architecture is championed by the Napier Museum and Thiruvananthapuram Zoo, one of the oldest zoos in India.[162] Other architectural landmarks include Kuthira Malika Palace, Kowdiar Palace, Attukal Bhagavathy Temple, Beemapally Mosque, Connemara Market, and the Mateer Memorial Church. Thiruvananthapuram was the main centre of Laurie Baker's architecture.[163]

Located on the west coast of India near the extreme south of the mainland, Thiruvananthapuram is a port city located 10 nautical miles (19 km; 12 mi)[15] from a heavily trafficked east–west shipping channel. The city is home to India's first deep-water trans-shipment port, owned by the Vizhinjam International Seaport Ltd. Thiruvananthapuram under the Government of Kerala.[16] The city is characterised by its undulating terrain of low coastal hills.[17] Thiruvananthapuram is also known for its cultural heritage, being associated with the musical contributions of Swathi Thirunal Rama Varma and the artistic legacy of painter Raja Ravi Varma. Thiruvananthapuram has contributed to the development of Malayalam literature through individuals like Ulloor S. Parameswara Iyer, Kumaran Asan, C. V. Raman Pillai and Narayana Guru. The city is also known for Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple, known as the richest temple in the world.[18] The other temples includes the Sreevaraham temple, the Shreekanteswaram temple and the Attukal Bhagavathy temple.
The present regions that constitute Thiruvananthapuram were ruled by the Ays who were related to feudatories of the Chera dynasty.[19] In the 12th century, it was conquered by the Kingdom of Venad.[19] In the 18th century, the king Marthanda Varma expanded the territory, founded the princely state of Travancore and made Thiruvananthapuram its capital.[20] Travancore became the most dominant state in Kerala by defeating the powerful Zamorin of Calicut in the battle of Purakkad in 1755.[21] Following India's independence in 1947, Thiruvananthapuram became the capital of Travancore–Cochin state and remained so until the new Indian state of Kerala was formed in 1956.[22][23]
texts.4:
Thiruvananthapuram is a notable academic and research hub and home to the University of Kerala, APJ Abdul Kalam Technological University, the regional headquarters of Indira Gandhi National Open University, and many other schools and colleges. Thiruvananthapuram is also home to research centres such as the National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology, the Indian Space Research Organisation's Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, the Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology, the National Centre for Earth Science Studies and a campus of the Indian Institutes of Science Education and Research.[24] Thiruvananthapuram is where India's space programme began, with the headquarters of Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre located there. The city is home to media institutions like Toonz Animation India and Tata Elxsi Ltd, and also to Chitranjali Film Studio, one of the first film studios in Malayalam Cinema, and Kinfra Film and Video Park at Kazhakoottam, which is India's first infotainment industrial park.[25]
In 2012, Thiruvananthapuram was named the best Kerala city to live in, by a field survey conducted by The Times of India.[26] In 2013, the city was ranked the fifteenth best city to live in in India, in a survey conducted by India Today.[27] Thiruvananthapuram was ranked the best Indian city for two consecutive years, 2015 and 2016, according to the Annual Survey of India's City-Systems (ASICS) conducted by the Janaagraha Centre for Citizenship and Democracy.[28] The city was also selected as the best governed city in India in a survey conducted by Janaagraha Centre for citizenship and democracy in 2017.[29]
Etymologyedit
texts.5:
The city takes its name from the Malayalam word thiru-anantha-puram (തിരുവനന്തപുരം [t̪iɾuʋɐnɐn̪d̪ɐpuɾɐm] ⓘ), meaning "The City of Lord Anantha (means infinite, endless, or eternal)",[30] referring to the deity of the Sri Padmanabhaswamy Temple located in the city. Thiruvananthapuram is also known in literature, and popular reference as Ananthapuri, derived from the Sanskrit word Syanandurapuram, meaning "The City of Bliss" in Carnatic kirtanas composed by Swathi Thirunal, erstwhile Maharaja of Travancore.[31] The city was officially referred to as Trivandrum until 1991 (Trivandrum being the anglicised name of the town), when the government decided to reinstate the city's original name Thiruvananthapuram. Many Malayalees still refer to the city as Trivandrum, however.[32] The city was also called as Anandapatnam or Anandapatam in Tamil and Telugu, meaning "The City of Ananda" which has the same meaning as the original name. [citation needed]
Historyedit  
Main article: History of Thiruvananthapuram  
See also: Merger of Kanyakumari with Madras State  
Painting by Raja Ravi Varma depicting Richard Temple-Grenville, 3rd Duke of Buckingham and Chandos being greeted by Visakham Thirunal, with Ayilyam Thirunal of Travancore looking on, during Buckingham's visit to Thiruvananthapuram in early 1880  
Padmanabhaswamy Temple is the richest temple in the world.  
Padmanabhapuram Palace  
Pre-historic periodedit
texts.6:
Thiruvananthapuram is a relatively modern region with trading traditions dating back to 1000 BCE.[33][34] It is believed that the ships of King Solomon landed in a port then called Ophir (now Poovar) in Thiruvananthapuram in 1036 BCE.[35][36] The city was the trading post for spices, sandalwood and ivory.[37] However, the ancient political and cultural history of the city was almost entirely independent from that of the rest of Kerala. [citation needed]
Ancient periodedit
The southern region of present-day Kerala state (The coastal belt between Thiruvananthapuram and Alappuzha) was under the Ay dynasty, which was more related to the Pandya dynasty of Madurai.[38][page needed] The early rulers of the city were the Ays. Vizhinjam, which is now a region in present-day Thiruvananthapuram, was the capital of the Ay dynasty.[39] Vizhinjam was an important port city from as early as the second century BC.[40][41] During the Ay dynasty's rule, Thiruvananthapuram witnessed many battles in which the Chola and Pandyan dynasties attempted to capture the port town.[42][43]
Middle Agesedit
After the death of king Vikramaditya Varaguna in 925 AD, the glory of the Ays departed and almost all their territories became part of the Chera dynasty.[44][19] During the tenth century, the Cholas attacked and sacked Vizhinjam and surrounding regions.[19] The port in Vizhinjam and the historic education centre of Kanthalloor Sala were also destroyed by Cholas during this period.[45][46] A branch of the Ay family, which had controlled the Padmanabhaswamy Temple, merged with the Kingdom of Venad in the 12th century.[19]
A map of Malabar Coast drawn by Homann Heirs in 1733. At that time, Travancore was only a small territory wedged between Kollam and Kanyakumari, as shown in the map (Present-day districts of Thiruvananthapuram and Kanyakumari only).  
Early Modern periodedit
texts.24:
Tourism is a significant economic sector.[127][128][129] The presence of natural attractions like beaches, backwaters, hills, and plantations and attractions like heritage, history, Ayurveda, medical tourism and knowledge centres attract many tourists.[130] The city experienced a surge of investment in the real estate, infrastructure and retail sectors in 2016–17.[131]
Port-based developmentedit
Thiruvananthapuram is a commercial port city with port-related infrastructure due to the presence of the Deepwater Container Transhipment port operated by the Vizhinjam International Seaport Ltd. Thiruvananthapuram.[132]
The port is located close to international shipping routes, approximately 10 to 12 nautical miles (19 to 22 km) from the busy Persian Gulf–Malacca shipping lane.[133] It has a natural depth of 18 to 20 metres (59 to 66 ft), enabling it to accommodate large container vessels.[134] The berths are designed to handle vessels of up to 24,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU).[135] Port-related development has been associated with increased activity in logistics, warehousing, shipping services and supporting infrastructure, trade and transport connectivity.[citation needed]
Trivandrum Outer Ring Roadedit
texts.25:
The proposed Trivandrum Outer Ring Road (ORR) (ORR), also known as the Outer Area Growth Corridor (OAGC), is a major infrastructure initiative aimed at supporting the long-term economic development of the city and its surrounding region. The corridor, extending approximately 78–80 km between Vizhinjam International Seaport Thiruvananthapuram and Navaikulam, is planned as a six-lane access-controlled highway with designated economic zones along its alignment. The TOAGC master plan envisages the development of multiple sector-specific clusters, including logistics, industrial development, information technology, healthcare, health tourism, general tourism, education, and commercial services, forming an integrated investment region around the capital area. Key nodes such as Vizhinjam, Kovalam, Vembayam, Mangalapuram, and Nedumangad have been identified for focused development, including a logistics hub at Vizhinjam and a health and tourism hub in the coastal belt. The project is also expected to strengthen connectivity between Vizhinjam International Seaport, the IT corridors, and the national highway network, thereby facilitating port-led industrial growth and regional economic expansion.[136][137][138]
Tourismedit  
Main article: Tourism in Thiruvananthapuram  
Harvesting lotus leaves from Vellayani Lake.
Thiruvananthapuram is a major tourist hub in India.[128] Kovalam and Varkala are popular beach towns near the city.[139] Other important beaches include Poovar, Shankumugham Beach, Azhimala Beach, Vizhinjam Beach and Veli Beach. Other places of interest include the Agasthyamala rain forests, Neyyar Wildlife Sanctuary, Kallar, Braemore, Ponmudi hills, Poovar, the Anchuthengu backwaters, Varkala Cliffs and Kappil-Edava lakes. [citation needed]
The city is also known for its unique style of architecture involving Kerala Architecture with British and Dravidian influences.[140] Napier museum, Thiruvanathapuram Zoo, Padmanabha Swamy temple, Kuthira Malika palace, Kilimanoor palace and The Thiruvananthapuram Golf Club heritage building are examples of this. [citation needed]
texts.26:
The main museums include the Kerala Science and Technology Museum (with its attached Priyadarsini Planetarium), the Napier Museum, the Kerala Soil Museum and the Koyikkal Palace Museum. Agasthyamala Biosphere Reserve is listed in UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves.[141]
Cultureedit  
Main article: Culture of Thiruvananthapuram  
Established in 1855, the Napier Museum contains a vast collection of Ancient paintings and archaeological artefacts
Thiruvananthapuram is known as the "Evergreen City of India" because of its green landscapes and the presence of many public parks.[142] Thiruvananthapuram has historically been a cultural hub in Southern India due to the development of arts, architecture and liberal customs by the rulers of erstwhile Thiruvananthapuram. As a testimony to this, renowned artists like Maharaja Swathi Thirunal and Raja Ravi Varma hail from the city.[143][144] Prominent social reformers such as Sri Narayana Guru, Chattampi Swamikal, Ayyankali, Vakkom Moulavi and C. V. Raman Pillai also are from Thiruvananthapuram.[145]
texts.27:
Two of the three Malayalam triumvirate poets, Ulloor S. Parameswara Iyer and Kumaran Asan are from Thiruvananthapuram.[146][147] Annual literature festivals like the Kovalam Literary Festival, are held in the city.[148] Literary development is further aided by state institutions such as the State Central Library, one of the oldest public libraries in India, which was established in 1829,[149] and other major libraries including the Thiruvananthapuram Corporation Central library, and the Kerala University Library.[150] Thiruvananthapuram has been a hub of classical music since the days of Maharaja of Travancore, Swathi Thirunal.[151][152] Thiruvananthapuram is known for many music festivals like the Navarathri Music Festival, one of the oldest festivals of its kind in South India,[151] Swathi Sangeethotsavam, Soorya Music fest, Neelakanta Sivan Music Fest and many other music festivals are organised by various cultural groups.[151] The 111-day-long Soorya Festival is the biggest art and cultural event in Kerala.[153][154] The Soorya Festival features film festivals, theatre festivals, dance, music, painting and photography exhibitions.[153]
16th IFFK 2011 banner at Kairali Theater Complex
texts.28:
The Malayalam film Industry was started in Thiruvananthapuram. The first Malayalam feature film, Vigathakumaran, directed by J. C. Daniel, was released in Thiruvananthapuram.[155] J. C. Daniel is considered the father of the Malayalam film industry. He also established the first film studio in Kerala, the Travancore National Pictures at Thiruvananthapuram in 1926.[156][157] The International Film Festival of Kerala (IFFK), which is held every year in December, is one of Asia's largest film festivals in terms of viewer participation.[158][159] In addition to various film festivals, the presence of the Central Board of Film Certification's regional office, many movie studios and production facilities like the Uma Studio, Chitranjali Studio, Merryland Studio, Kinfra Film and Video Park and Vismayas Max contribute to the growth of Thiruvananthapuram as a centre of cinema.[160][161]
Apart from the famous Padmanabhaswamy Temple, the city's architecture is championed by the Napier Museum and Thiruvananthapuram Zoo, one of the oldest zoos in India.[162] Other architectural landmarks include Kuthira Malika Palace, Kowdiar Palace, Attukal Bhagavathy Temple, Beemapally Mosque, Connemara Market, and the Mateer Memorial Church. Thiruvananthapuram was the main centre of Laurie Baker's architecture.[163]

**Shashi Tharoor** (Malayalam pronunciation:[[ʃɐʃi t̪ɐɾuːr]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Malayalam "Help:IPA/Malayalam"); born 9 March 1956) is an Indian politician, civil servant, author, public intellectual, diplomat, and bureaucrat.. A member of the [Indian National Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_National_Congress "Indian National Congress"), he has represented [Thiruvananthapuram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_(Lok_Sabha_constituency) "Thiruvananthapuram (Lok Sabha constituency)"), [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala"), in the [Lok Sabha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lok_Sabha "Lok Sabha") since 2009. He was formerly an [Under-Secretary-General of the United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under-Secretary-General_of_the_United_Nations "Under-Secretary-General of the United Nations") and ran for the office of [Secretary-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary-General_of_the_United_Nations "Secretary-General of the United Nations") in 2006, coming second.

## Political career (2009–present)
### In government (2009–2014)
Between 2010 and 2012, Tharoor remained active in Parliament and was member-convenor of the Parliamentary Forum on Disaster Management, a member of the Standing Committee on External Affairs, of the Consultative Committee of Defence, [the Public Accounts Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Accounts_Committee "Public Accounts Committee"), and the Joint Parliamentary Committee on Telecoms. He participated in several important debates of the 15th Lok Sabha, including on the Lokpal Bill, the demand for grants of the Ministry of External Affairs and of the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, the black money debate, and so on. In the special debate on the 60th anniversary of the Indian Parliament, Tharoor was one of four members of the Congress Party, including party President [Sonia Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonia_Gandhi "Sonia Gandhi"), Prime Minister Manmohan Singh, and Leader of the House [Pranab Mukherjee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pranab_Mukherjee "Pranab Mukherjee"), to be invited to address the Lok Sabha.
In 2012, Tharoor was re-inducted into the Union Council of Ministers by Prime Minister Manmohan Singh with the portfolio of [minister of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_state "Minister of state") for [Human Resource Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Education_(India) "Ministry of Education (India)"). In this role, he took special interest in the problems and challenges of [adult education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_education "Adult education"), [distance education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance_education "Distance education") and enhancing high-quality research by academic institutions. He was responsible for the ministry's written answers to Parliament's questions and responded to oral questions on education during the Lok Sabha's Question Hour. He addressed forums and conferences on education, explained a vision of India's educational challenges in the context of the country's demographic opportunities, and stressed that education was not only a socioeconomic issue, but also a national security issue.

## Political career (2009–present)
### In government (2009–2014)
As Member of Parliament for [Thiruvananthapuram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_district "Thiruvananthapuram district"), Tharoor became the first elected representative in India to issue annual reports on his work as MP, including furnishing accounts of his MPLADS expenditure. In 2012, he published a half-term report followed in 2014 by a full-term report.

## Political career (2009–present)

In regards to Tharoor's removal from the post of INC spokesperson after he made positive remarks regarding Narendra Modi, Kolkata's _[The Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Telegraph\_(Kolkata) "The Telegraph (Kolkata)")_ opined, "For an Opposition MP to have and to exercise the freedom to appreciate a good thing done by the government and for a ruling party MP to speak and vote against the party line is not just legitimate parliamentary practice, it is the very essence of parliamentary democracy. Shashi Tharoor, from the ranks of Congress, has tried to do that; there is not one BJP MP who has matched him. Blind conformism is not loyalty, nor independent thinking, dissent."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-33)
In 2014, Tharoor was asked to help the treasury benches draft a statement condemning Pakistan for freeing Zaki-ur-Rehman Lakhvi, the Lashkar-e-Toiba commander, who masterminded the [2008 Mumbai attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Mumbai_attacks "2008 Mumbai attacks") that killed 166 people. ## Political career (2009–present)
### In opposition (2014–present)
In March 2017, Tharoor called for the [Victoria Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Memorial,_Kolkata "Victoria Memorial, Kolkata") in [Kolkata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolkata "Kolkata") to be converted into a museum on the effects of [British colonial rule in India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj "British Raj"). Tharoor wrote in an _[Al Jazeera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al\_Jazeera\_English "Al Jazeera English")_ article that the British "conquered one of the richest countries in the world (27 per cent of global gross domestic product in 1700) and reduced it to, after over two centuries of looting and exploitation, one of the poorest, most diseased and most illiterate countries on Earth by the time they left in 1947. ...Nor is there any memorial to the massacres of the Raj, from Delhi in 1857 to [Amritsar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jallianwala_Bagh_massacre "Jallianwala Bagh massacre") in 1919, the [deaths of 35 million Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_major_famines_in_India_during_British_rule "Timeline of major famines in India during British rule") in unnecessary [famines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famine_in_India "Famine in India") caused by British [policies]".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-39)
He declined and dismissed any suggestions regarding the potential of him being named as the UPA's prime ministerial candidate in [2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Indian_general_election "2019 Indian general election").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-41)

**[Thiruvananthapuram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram "Thiruvananthapuram") Parliamentary (Lok Sabha) Constituency** is one of the 20 parliamentary constituencies in Kerala, India. It is located in [Thiruvananthapuram district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_district "Thiruvananthapuram district") and encompasses the major part of [Thiruvananthapuram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram "Thiruvananthapuram") city, the capital of [Kerala State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala").

The incumbent MP of this constituency, [Shashi Tharoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor "Shashi Tharoor") of the [Indian National Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_National_Congress "Indian National Congress"), has been elected on 4 consecutive occasions: 2009, 2014, 2019 and 2024. He is the longest serving Member of Parliament to have represented the constituency.
This constituency is dominated By [Nair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nair "Nair") and [Nadar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadar_(caste) "Nadar (caste)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_(Lok_Sabha_constituency)#cite_note-2) As per the electoral roll for the 2024 polls, the total electorate is of 14,03,281 people including 7,27,469 women, 6,75,771 men and 41 transgender people.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_(Lok_Sabha_constituency)#cite_note-3) Out of total electorate, 26% is rural and 74% is urban.

The Scheduled castes (SC) and Scheduled tribes (ST) is 9.82% and 0.45%, respectively of total electorate.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_(Lok_Sabha_constituency)#cite_note-4) The constituency also has highest proportion of [Nadars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadar_(caste) "Nadar (caste)") and [Converted Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversion_to_Christianity "Conversion to Christianity") in Kerala.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_(Lok_Sabha_constituency)#cite_note-5)[Nairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nair "Nair") dominates the urban segments of [Kazhakootam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazhakootam_Assembly_constituency "Kazhakootam Assembly constituency"),[Nemom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nemom_Assembly_constituency "Nemom Assembly constituency"),[Vattiyoorkavu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vattiyoorkavu_Assembly_constituency "Vattiyoorkavu Assembly constituency") and [Thiruvananthapuram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_Assembly_constituency "Thiruvananthapuram Assembly constituency") While the [Nadars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadar_(caste) "Nadar (caste)") are Concentrated on [Neyyattinkara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neyyattinkara_Assembly_constituency "Neyyattinkara Assembly constituency"),[Parassala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parassala_Assembly_constituency "Parassala Assembly constituency"),[Kovalam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kovalam_Assembly_constituency "Kovalam Assembly constituency").

As per the voter list published by the Election commission for the 2019 Lok Sabha elections, there were 13,34,665 voters in the electorate and 1077 polling stations in this constituency.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_(Lok_Sabha_constituency)#cite_note-ceo.kerala.gov.in-6) The voter turnout for the 2019 Lok Sabha election was 73.45% where as it was 68.63% and 65.74% in the 2014 and 2009 elections respectively.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_(Lok_Sabha_constituency)#cite_note-7)

texts.6: **Shashi Tharoor** (Malayalam pronunciation:[[ʃɐʃi t̪ɐɾuːr]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Malayalam "Help:IPA/Malayalam"); born 9 March 1956) is an Indian politician, civil servant, author, public intellectual, diplomat, and bureaucrat.. A member of the [Indian National Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_National_Congress "Indian National Congress"), he has represented [Thiruvananthapuram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_(Lok_Sabha_constituency) "Thiruvananthapuram (Lok Sabha constituency)"), [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala"), in the [Lok Sabha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lok_Sabha "Lok Sabha") since 2009. He was formerly an [Under-Secretary-General of the United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under-Secretary-General_of_the_United_Nations "Under-Secretary-General of the United Nations") and ran for the office of [Secretary-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary-General_of_the_United_Nations "Secretary-General of the United Nations") in 2006, coming second.

## Political career (2009–present)
### In government (2009–2014)
Between 2010 and 2012, Tharoor remained active in Parliament and was member-convenor of the Parliamentary Forum on Disaster Management, a member of the Standing Committee on External Affairs, of the Consultative Committee of Defence, [the Public Accounts Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Accounts_Committee "Public Accounts Committee"), and the Joint Parliamentary Committee on Telecoms. He participated in several important debates of the 15th Lok Sabha, including on the Lokpal Bill, the demand for grants of the Ministry of External Affairs and of the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, the black money debate, and so on. In the special debate on the 60th anniversary of the Indian Parliament, Tharoor was one of four members of the Congress Party, including party President [Sonia Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonia_Gandhi "Sonia Gandhi"), Prime Minister Manmohan Singh, and Leader of the House [Pranab Mukherjee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pranab_Mukherjee "Pranab Mukherjee"), to be invited to address the Lok Sabha.
In 2012, Tharoor was re-inducted into the Union Council of Ministers by Prime Minister Manmohan Singh with the portfolio of [minister of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_state "Minister of state") for [Human Resource Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Education_(India) "Ministry of Education (India)"). In this role, he took special interest in the problems and challenges of [adult education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_education "Adult education"), [distance education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance_education "Distance education") and enhancing high-quality research by academic institutions. He was responsible for the ministry's written answers to Parliament's questions and responded to oral questions on education during the Lok Sabha's Question Hour. He addressed forums and conferences on education, explained a vision of India's educational challenges in the context of the country's demographic opportunities, and stressed that education was not only a socioeconomic issue, but also a national security issue.

In regards to Tharoor's removal from the post of INC spokesperson after he made positive remarks regarding Narendra Modi, Kolkata's _[The Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Telegraph\_(Kolkata) "The Telegraph (Kolkata)")_ opined, "For an Opposition MP to have and to exercise the freedom to appreciate a good thing done by the government and for a ruling party MP to speak and vote against the party line is not just legitimate parliamentary practice, it is the very essence of parliamentary democracy. Shashi Tharoor, from the ranks of Congress, has tried to do that; there is not one BJP MP who has matched him. Blind conformism is not loyalty, nor independent thinking, dissent."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-33)
In 2014, Tharoor was asked to help the treasury benches draft a statement condemning Pakistan for freeing Zaki-ur-Rehman Lakhvi, the Lashkar-e-Toiba commander, who masterminded the [2008 Mumbai attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Mumbai_attacks "2008 Mumbai attacks") that killed 166 people. In January 2015, Tharoor asked not to debunk genuine accomplishments of Ancient Indian Science due to exaggerations of the [Hindutva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindutva "Hindutva") brigade,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-36) amid [2015 Indian Science Congress ancient aircraft controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Indian_Science_Congress_ancient_aircraft_controversy "2015 Indian Science Congress ancient aircraft controversy").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-38)

In March 2017, Tharoor called for the [Victoria Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Memorial,_Kolkata "Victoria Memorial, Kolkata") in [Kolkata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolkata "Kolkata") to be converted into a museum on the effects of [British colonial rule in India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj "British Raj"). Tharoor wrote in an _[Al Jazeera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al\_Jazeera\_English "Al Jazeera English")_ article that the British "conquered one of the richest countries in the world (27 per cent of global gross domestic product in 1700) and reduced it to, after over two centuries of looting and exploitation, one of the poorest, most diseased and most illiterate countries on Earth by the time they left in 1947. ...Nor is there any memorial to the massacres of the Raj, from Delhi in 1857 to [Amritsar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jallianwala_Bagh_massacre "Jallianwala Bagh massacre") in 1919, the [deaths of 35 million Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_major_famines_in_India_during_British_rule "Timeline of major famines in India during British rule") in unnecessary [famines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famine_in_India "Famine in India") caused by British [policies]".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-39)
He declined and dismissed any suggestions regarding the potential of him being named as the UPA's prime ministerial candidate in [2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Indian_general_election "2019 Indian general election").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-41)

He termed the opportunity as a "great honour" and a "matter of duty" as a citizen of India and said he looks forward to playing his part in leading the delegation even as his party, Congress, has frowned upon his inclusion. He asserted that only national interest is above everything else.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-55) Tharoor explicitly identified Pakistan as the principal perpetrator. He emphasized in diplomatic briefings and public statements that the attack was carried out by militants linked to Lashkar-e-Taiba, operating with Pakistan's support, and stressed that India's response targeted only terrorist infrastructure.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-58) During the delegation's visit to the [9/11 Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_September_11_Memorial_&_Museum "National September 11 Memorial & Museum") in New York, Tharoor highlighted the shared experience of India and the US as victims of terrorism and called for global solidarity in holding state sponsors of terror accountable.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor#cite_note-60)

Thiruvananthapuram (Malayalam pronunciation: [t̪iɾuʋənən̪d̪ɐˈbuɾəm] ⓘ tirr-ROO-və-nun-Tə-poor-əm), also known as Trivandrum, is the capital city of the Indian state of Kerala.[9][10] As of 2011, the Thiruvananthapuram Municipal Corporation had a population of 957,730 over an area of 214.86 km2,[11] making it the most populous city in Kerala.[12] The larger Thiruvananthapuram metropolitan area has over 1.7 million inhabitants within an area of 543 km2, making it the second-most populous metropolitan area in Kerala after Kochi.[13]. Thiruvananthapuram is one of the few cities in India that serves as a state capital and is also centre for heritage, maritime activities, information technology, research and development, space research, defence, automotive technology, and biosciences. It is also among the few cities in the world where both an international airport and an international seaport are located within the city in close proximity to the city centre.[14]

Located on the west coast of India near the extreme south of the mainland, Thiruvananthapuram is a port city located 10 nautical miles (19 km; 12 mi)[15] from a heavily trafficked east–west shipping channel. The city is home to India's first deep-water trans-shipment port, owned by the Vizhinjam International Seaport Ltd. Thiruvananthapuram under the Government of Kerala.[16] The city is characterised by its undulating terrain of low coastal hills.[17] Thiruvananthapuram is also known for its cultural heritage, being associated with the musical contributions of Swathi Thirunal Rama Varma and the artistic legacy of painter Raja Ravi Varma. Thiruvananthapuram has contributed to the development of Malayalam literature through individuals like Ulloor S. Parameswara Iyer, Kumaran Asan, C. V. Raman Pillai and Narayana Guru. The city is also known for Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple, known as the richest temple in the world.[18] The other temples includes the Sreevaraham temple, the Shreekanteswaram temple and the Attukal Bhagavathy temple.
The present regions that constitute Thiruvananthapuram were ruled by the Ays who were related to feudatories of the Chera dynasty.[19] In the 12th century, it was conquered by the Kingdom of Venad.[19] In the 18th century, the king Marthanda Varma expanded the territory, founded the princely state of Travancore and made Thiruvananthapuram its capital.[20] Travancore became the most dominant state in Kerala by defeating the powerful Zamorin of Calicut in the battle of Purakkad in 1755.[21] Following India's independence in 1947, Thiruvananthapuram became the capital of Travancore–Cochin state and remained so until the new Indian state of Kerala was formed in 1956.[22][23]

Thiruvananthapuram is a notable academic and research hub and home to the University of Kerala, APJ Abdul Kalam Technological University, the regional headquarters of Indira Gandhi National Open University, and many other schools and colleges. Thiruvananthapuram is also home to research centres such as the National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology, the Indian Space Research Organisation's Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, the Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology, the National Centre for Earth Science Studies and a campus of the Indian Institutes of Science Education and Research.[24] Thiruvananthapuram is where India's space programme began, with the headquarters of Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre located there. The city is home to media institutions like Toonz Animation India and Tata Elxsi Ltd, and also to Chitranjali Film Studio, one of the first film studios in Malayalam Cinema, and Kinfra Film and Video Park at Kazhakoottam, which is India's first infotainment industrial park.[25]
In 2012, Thiruvananthapuram was named the best Kerala city to live in, by a field survey conducted by The Times of India.[26] In 2013, the city was ranked the fifteenth best city to live in in India, in a survey conducted by India Today.[27] Thiruvananthapuram was ranked the best Indian city for two consecutive years, 2015 and 2016, according to the Annual Survey of India's City-Systems (ASICS) conducted by the Janaagraha Centre for Citizenship and Democracy.[28] The city was also selected as the best governed city in India in a survey conducted by Janaagraha Centre for citizenship and democracy in 2017.[29]
Etymologyedit

The city takes its name from the Malayalam word thiru-anantha-puram (തിരുവനന്തപുരം [t̪iɾuʋɐnɐn̪d̪ɐpuɾɐm] ⓘ), meaning "The City of Lord Anantha (means infinite, endless, or eternal)",[30] referring to the deity of the Sri Padmanabhaswamy Temple located in the city. Thiruvananthapuram is also known in literature, and popular reference as Ananthapuri, derived from the Sanskrit word Syanandurapuram, meaning "The City of Bliss" in Carnatic kirtanas composed by Swathi Thirunal, erstwhile Maharaja of Travancore.[31] The city was officially referred to as Trivandrum until 1991 (Trivandrum being the anglicised name of the town), when the government decided to reinstate the city's original name Thiruvananthapuram. Many Malayalees still refer to the city as Trivandrum, however.[32] The city was also called as Anandapatnam or Anandapatam in Tamil and Telugu, meaning "The City of Ananda" which has the same meaning as the original name. [citation needed]
Historyedit  
Main article: History of Thiruvananthapuram  
See also: Merger of Kanyakumari with Madras State  
Painting by Raja Ravi Varma depicting Richard Temple-Grenville, 3rd Duke of Buckingham and Chandos being greeted by Visakham Thirunal, with Ayilyam Thirunal of Travancore looking on, during Buckingham's visit to Thiruvananthapuram in early 1880  
Padmanabhaswamy Temple is the richest temple in the world.  
Padmanabhapuram Palace  
Pre-historic periodedit

Thiruvananthapuram is a relatively modern region with trading traditions dating back to 1000 BCE.[33][34] It is believed that the ships of King Solomon landed in a port then called Ophir (now Poovar) in Thiruvananthapuram in 1036 BCE.[35][36] The city was the trading post for spices, sandalwood and ivory.[37] However, the ancient political and cultural history of the city was almost entirely independent from that of the rest of Kerala. [citation needed]
Ancient periodedit
The southern region of present-day Kerala state (The coastal belt between Thiruvananthapuram and Alappuzha) was under the Ay dynasty, which was more related to the Pandya dynasty of Madurai.[38][page needed] The early rulers of the city were the Ays. Vizhinjam, which is now a region in present-day Thiruvananthapuram, was the capital of the Ay dynasty.[39] Vizhinjam was an important port city from as early as the second century BC.[40][41] During the Ay dynasty's rule, Thiruvananthapuram witnessed many battles in which the Chola and Pandyan dynasties attempted to capture the port town.[42][43]
Middle Agesedit
After the death of king Vikramaditya Varaguna in 925 AD, the glory of the Ays departed and almost all their territories became part of the Chera dynasty.[44][19] During the tenth century, the Cholas attacked and sacked Vizhinjam and surrounding regions.[19] The port in Vizhinjam and the historic education centre of Kanthalloor Sala were also destroyed by Cholas during this period.[45][46] A branch of the Ay family, which had controlled the Padmanabhaswamy Temple, merged with the Kingdom of Venad in the 12th century.[19]

**Raja Ravi Varma** (Malayalam:[[ɾaːd͡ʒaː ɾɐʋi ʋɐrmːɐ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Malayalam "Help:IPA/Malayalam")) (29 April 1848 – 2 October 1906[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-4)) was an Indian painter. His works are one of the best examples of the fusion of European [academic art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_art "Academic art") with a purely Indian sensibility and iconography. He greatly enhanced his reach and influence as a painter and public figure by making affordable [lithographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithography "Lithography") of his paintings available to the public. His lithographs increased the involvement of common people with fine arts and defined artistic tastes. His religious depictions of Hindu deities and works from [Indian epic poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_epic_poetry "Indian epic poetry") and [Puranas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puranas "Puranas") have received critical acclaim. He was part of the royal family of [Parappanad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parappanad "Parappanad"), [Malappuram district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malappuram_district "Malappuram district").
Raja Ravi Varma was closely related to the royal family of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore") of present-day [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala") state in India. Later in his life, two of his granddaughters were adopted into the royal family.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-5)

The title [Raja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja "Raja") was conferred as a personal title by the Viceroy and Governor-General of India [Lord Curzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Curzon "Lord Curzon").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-pal-6)

Varma's sister-in-law, [Bharani Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharani_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi "Bharani Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi"), Senior Rani of [Attingal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal "Attingal") (or [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Travancore "Kingdom of Travancore")), who adopted Varma's granddaughters in 1900

Ravi Varma was the son of Ezhumavil Neelakanthan Bhattatiripad and Uma Ambabayi Thampurratti. His mother Uma Ambabayi Thampuratty belonged to the baronial family which ruled the Kilimanoor [feudal estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") within the kingdom of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore"). She was a poet and writer, and her work _Parvati Swayamvaram_ was published by Varma after her death. Ravi Varma's father was a scholar of [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit "Sanskrit") and [Ayurveda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayurveda "Ayurveda") and hailed from the [Ernakulam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernakulam "Ernakulam") district in Kerala. Ravi Varma had two siblings, a sister named [Mangala Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mangala_Bayi "Mangala Bayi") and a brother named [Raja Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Raja_Raja_Varma "C. Raja Raja Varma") (born 1860). The last-named was also a painter and worked closely with Ravi Varma all his life.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1866, at age 18, Varma was married to 12-year-old Bhageerthi Bayi (known formally as Pooruruttati Nal Bhageerathi Bayi Thampuratty) of the royal house of [Mavelikkara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mavelikkara "Mavelikkara"), another major [fief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") of Travancore kingdom. Notably, the house of Mavellikara was a branch of the Royal House of Travancore. Bhageerthi was the youngest of three sisters; her two elder siblings were adopted into the royal family of Travancore in 1857 to perpetuate the lineage. Designated the Senior and Junior Rani of Attingal, their descendants were vested with the succession to the throne of Travancore. Therefore, Ravi Varma's connection to the royal family became very close due to his marriage with Bhageerthi. His children would be royal by birth, since they belonged to their mother's family. The marriage, which was arranged by the parents in the proper Indian manner, was considered successful. The couple had five children, two sons, and three daughters. Their elder son, Kerala Varma (b.1876) was of an excessively spiritual temperament. He never married and eventually renounced the world, leaving home for good in 1912. The younger son, Rama Varma (born 1879), inherited his father's artistic talent and studied at the [JJ School of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JJ_School_of_Arts "JJ School of Arts"), [Mumbai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumbai "Mumbai"). He was married to Gowri Kunjamma, sister of [Dewan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewan "Dewan")[PGN Unnithan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PGN_Unnithan "PGN Unnithan"), and became the father of seven children.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The three daughters of Ravi Varma and Bhageerthi Bayi were Mahaprabha Amma (who features in two of Varma's most famous paintings), Uma Amma (named after Varma's mother) and Cheria Kochamma. In 1900 CE, the Royal House of Travancore once again faced a succession crisis. Bhageerthi's two elder sisters, who had been adopted in order to carry forward the lineage, had failed to produce the desired heirs. They had six children between them, but only two of those survived, and both were boys (who also, incidentally, later died childless). According to the [matrilineal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrilineal "Matrilineal") Marumakkathayam system, the succession to the throne could only progress through females, and therefore it was necessary to make an adoption. Tradition dictated that two girls belonging to branches of the Royal Family be adopted together. They would be designated the Senior and Junior Rani of Attingal, and the succession to the throne of Travancore would be vested in their progeny, in accordance with the unusual and unique [Marumakkathayam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marumakkathayam "Marumakkathayam") system of succession.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Two of Varma's granddaughters were marked by destiny to receive this honour, the main reason being that they were the nearest matrilineal ([cognatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognatic "Cognatic")) kin to the incumbent Rani of Attingal. In August 1900, Mahaprabha's eldest daughter Lakshmi Bayi (aged 5 years) and Uma's eldest daughter Parvati Bayi (aged 4 years) were adopted into the Royal family of Travancore. It was [Bharani Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharani_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi "Bharani Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi"), their surviving grand-aunt, who formally adopted them. She died within one year of doing this, and the two girls were then installed as the Senior and Junior Ranis of [Attingal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal "Attingal") respectively. They were married while yet in their early teens to two gentlemen from suitable aristocratic families. It was the Junior Rani, [Sethu Parvathi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sethu_Parvathi_Bayi "Sethu Parvathi Bayi"), who gave birth to the much-awaited heir in 1912, exactly a day after her sixteenth birthday. Incidentally, her husband was a grand-nephew of Raja Ravi Varma and belonged to [Kilimanoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor_Palace "Kilimanoor Palace"). The newborn child was the future Maharaja [Chithira Thirunal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chithira_Thirunal_Balarama_Varma "Chithira Thirunal Balarama Varma"), the last ruling [Maharaja of Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maharaja_of_Travancore "Maharaja of Travancore").

He was followed by a brother (the future Maharaja [Marthanda Varma III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uthradom_Thirunal_Marthanda_Varma "Uthradom Thirunal Marthanda Varma")) and a sister [Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karthika_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi "Karthika Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi"), the mother of Maharaja [Rama Varma VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moolam_Thirunal_Rama_Varma "Moolam Thirunal Rama Varma") who is presently on the throne (since 2013). Meanwhile, the Senior Rani ([Sethu Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sethu_Lakshmi_Bayi "Sethu Lakshmi Bayi"), daughter of Mahaprabha Amma, and Regent from 1924 to 1931) also gave birth to two daughters later in life (in 1923 and 1926).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
In this way, the entire present (existing) royal family of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore") is descended from Raja Ravi Varma. Well known among his royal descendants are the writers [Aswathi Thirunal Gowri Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswathi_Thirunal_Gowri_Lakshmi_Bayi "Aswathi Thirunal Gowri Lakshmi Bayi") and [Shreekumar Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shreekumar_Varma "Shreekumar Varma"), the artist [Rukmini Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rukmini_Varma "Rukmini Varma") and the classical musician [Aswathi Thirunal Rama Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswathi_Thirunal_Rama_Varma "Aswathi Thirunal Rama Varma").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Around Ravi Varma's 57th birthday he announced his decision to accept [Sanyasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanyasa "Sanyasa"), and retire from all worldly life when he turned 60. In his final years he suffered from grief for the death of Raja Raja Varma, and also from diabetes, which contributed to his death on 2 October 1906.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
Varma was patronised by [Ayilyam Thirunal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayilyam_Thirunal "Ayilyam Thirunal"), the next [Maharaja of Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maharaja_of_Travancore "Maharaja of Travancore") and began formal training thereafter.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-The_Diary_of_C._Rajaraja_Varma-7) He learned the basics of painting in [Madurai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madurai "Madurai"). Later, he was trained in water painting by Rama Swami Naidu and rather reluctantly in [oil painting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_painting "Oil painting") by British portraitist Theodore Jenson.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-8)

Located on the west coast of India near the extreme south of the mainland, Thiruvananthapuram is a port city located 10 nautical miles (19 km; 12 mi)[15] from a heavily trafficked east–west shipping channel. The city is home to India's first deep-water trans-shipment port, owned by the Vizhinjam International Seaport Ltd. Thiruvananthapuram under the Government of Kerala.[16] The city is characterised by its undulating terrain of low coastal hills.[17] Thiruvananthapuram is also known for its cultural heritage, being associated with the musical contributions of Swathi Thirunal Rama Varma and the artistic legacy of painter Raja Ravi Varma. Thiruvananthapuram has contributed to the development of Malayalam literature through individuals like Ulloor S. Parameswara Iyer, Kumaran Asan, C. V. Raman Pillai and Narayana Guru. The city is also known for Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple, known as the richest temple in the world.[18] The other temples includes the Sreevaraham temple, the Shreekanteswaram temple and the Attukal Bhagavathy temple.
The present regions that constitute Thiruvananthapuram were ruled by the Ays who were related to feudatories of the Chera dynasty.[19] In the 12th century, it was conquered by the Kingdom of Venad.[19] In the 18th century, the king Marthanda Varma expanded the territory, founded the princely state of Travancore and made Thiruvananthapuram its capital.[20] Travancore became the most dominant state in Kerala by defeating the powerful Zamorin of Calicut in the battle of Purakkad in 1755.[21] Following India's independence in 1947, Thiruvananthapuram became the capital of Travancore–Cochin state and remained so until the new Indian state of Kerala was formed in 1956.[22][23]

Thiruvananthapuram is a notable academic and research hub and home to the University of Kerala, APJ Abdul Kalam Technological University, the regional headquarters of Indira Gandhi National Open University, and many other schools and colleges. Thiruvananthapuram is also home to research centres such as the National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology, the Indian Space Research Organisation's Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, the Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology, the National Centre for Earth Science Studies and a campus of the Indian Institutes of Science Education and Research.[24] Thiruvananthapuram is where India's space programme began, with the headquarters of Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre located there. The city is home to media institutions like Toonz Animation India and Tata Elxsi Ltd, and also to Chitranjali Film Studio, one of the first film studios in Malayalam Cinema, and Kinfra Film and Video Park at Kazhakoottam, which is India's first infotainment industrial park.[25]
In 2012, Thiruvananthapuram was named the best Kerala city to live in, by a field survey conducted by The Times of India.[26] In 2013, the city was ranked the fifteenth best city to live in in India, in a survey conducted by India Today.[27] Thiruvananthapuram was ranked the best Indian city for two consecutive years, 2015 and 2016, according to the Annual Survey of India's City-Systems (ASICS) conducted by the Janaagraha Centre for Citizenship and Democracy.[28] The city was also selected as the best governed city in India in a survey conducted by Janaagraha Centre for citizenship and democracy in 2017.[29]
Etymologyedit

The city takes its name from the Malayalam word thiru-anantha-puram (തിരുവനന്തപുരം [t̪iɾuʋɐnɐn̪d̪ɐpuɾɐm] ⓘ), meaning "The City of Lord Anantha (means infinite, endless, or eternal)",[30] referring to the deity of the Sri Padmanabhaswamy Temple located in the city. Thiruvananthapuram is also known in literature, and popular reference as Ananthapuri, derived from the Sanskrit word Syanandurapuram, meaning "The City of Bliss" in Carnatic kirtanas composed by Swathi Thirunal, erstwhile Maharaja of Travancore.[31] The city was officially referred to as Trivandrum until 1991 (Trivandrum being the anglicised name of the town), when the government decided to reinstate the city's original name Thiruvananthapuram. Many Malayalees still refer to the city as Trivandrum, however.[32] The city was also called as Anandapatnam or Anandapatam in Tamil and Telugu, meaning "The City of Ananda" which has the same meaning as the original name. [citation needed]
Historyedit  
Main article: History of Thiruvananthapuram  
See also: Merger of Kanyakumari with Madras State  
Painting by Raja Ravi Varma depicting Richard Temple-Grenville, 3rd Duke of Buckingham and Chandos being greeted by Visakham Thirunal, with Ayilyam Thirunal of Travancore looking on, during Buckingham's visit to Thiruvananthapuram in early 1880  
Padmanabhaswamy Temple is the richest temple in the world.  
Padmanabhapuram Palace  
Pre-historic periodedit

Thiruvananthapuram is a relatively modern region with trading traditions dating back to 1000 BCE.[33][34] It is believed that the ships of King Solomon landed in a port then called Ophir (now Poovar) in Thiruvananthapuram in 1036 BCE.[35][36] The city was the trading post for spices, sandalwood and ivory.[37] However, the ancient political and cultural history of the city was almost entirely independent from that of the rest of Kerala. [citation needed]
Ancient periodedit
The southern region of present-day Kerala state (The coastal belt between Thiruvananthapuram and Alappuzha) was under the Ay dynasty, which was more related to the Pandya dynasty of Madurai.[38][page needed] The early rulers of the city were the Ays. Vizhinjam, which is now a region in present-day Thiruvananthapuram, was the capital of the Ay dynasty.[39] Vizhinjam was an important port city from as early as the second century BC.[40][41] During the Ay dynasty's rule, Thiruvananthapuram witnessed many battles in which the Chola and Pandyan dynasties attempted to capture the port town.[42][43]
Middle Agesedit
After the death of king Vikramaditya Varaguna in 925 AD, the glory of the Ays departed and almost all their territories became part of the Chera dynasty.[44][19] During the tenth century, the Cholas attacked and sacked Vizhinjam and surrounding regions.[19] The port in Vizhinjam and the historic education centre of Kanthalloor Sala were also destroyed by Cholas during this period.[45][46] A branch of the Ay family, which had controlled the Padmanabhaswamy Temple, merged with the Kingdom of Venad in the 12th century.[19]
A map of Malabar Coast drawn by Homann Heirs in 1733. At that time, Travancore was only a small territory wedged between Kollam and Kanyakumari, as shown in the map (Present-day districts of Thiruvananthapuram and Kanyakumari only).  
Early Modern periodedit

Tourism is a significant economic sector.[127][128][129] The presence of natural attractions like beaches, backwaters, hills, and plantations and attractions like heritage, history, Ayurveda, medical tourism and knowledge centres attract many tourists.[130] The city experienced a surge of investment in the real estate, infrastructure and retail sectors in 2016–17.[131]
Port-based developmentedit
Thiruvananthapuram is a commercial port city with port-related infrastructure due to the presence of the Deepwater Container Transhipment port operated by the Vizhinjam International Seaport Ltd. Thiruvananthapuram.[132]
The port is located close to international shipping routes, approximately 10 to 12 nautical miles (19 to 22 km) from the busy Persian Gulf–Malacca shipping lane.[133] It has a natural depth of 18 to 20 metres (59 to 66 ft), enabling it to accommodate large container vessels.[134] The berths are designed to handle vessels of up to 24,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU).[135] Port-related development has been associated with increased activity in logistics, warehousing, shipping services and supporting infrastructure, trade and transport connectivity.[citation needed]
Trivandrum Outer Ring Roadedit

The proposed Trivandrum Outer Ring Road (ORR) (ORR), also known as the Outer Area Growth Corridor (OAGC), is a major infrastructure initiative aimed at supporting the long-term economic development of the city and its surrounding region. The corridor, extending approximately 78–80 km between Vizhinjam International Seaport Thiruvananthapuram and Navaikulam, is planned as a six-lane access-controlled highway with designated economic zones along its alignment. The TOAGC master plan envisages the development of multiple sector-specific clusters, including logistics, industrial development, information technology, healthcare, health tourism, general tourism, education, and commercial services, forming an integrated investment region around the capital area. Key nodes such as Vizhinjam, Kovalam, Vembayam, Mangalapuram, and Nedumangad have been identified for focused development, including a logistics hub at Vizhinjam and a health and tourism hub in the coastal belt. The project is also expected to strengthen connectivity between Vizhinjam International Seaport, the IT corridors, and the national highway network, thereby facilitating port-led industrial growth and regional economic expansion.[136][137][138]
Tourismedit  
Main article: Tourism in Thiruvananthapuram  
Harvesting lotus leaves from Vellayani Lake.
Thiruvananthapuram is a major tourist hub in India.[128] Kovalam and Varkala are popular beach towns near the city.[139] Other important beaches include Poovar, Shankumugham Beach, Azhimala Beach, Vizhinjam Beach and Veli Beach. Other places of interest include the Agasthyamala rain forests, Neyyar Wildlife Sanctuary, Kallar, Braemore, Ponmudi hills, Poovar, the Anchuthengu backwaters, Varkala Cliffs and Kappil-Edava lakes. [citation needed]
The city is also known for its unique style of architecture involving Kerala Architecture with British and Dravidian influences.[140] Napier museum, Thiruvanathapuram Zoo, Padmanabha Swamy temple, Kuthira Malika palace, Kilimanoor palace and The Thiruvananthapuram Golf Club heritage building are examples of this. [citation needed]

The main museums include the Kerala Science and Technology Museum (with its attached Priyadarsini Planetarium), the Napier Museum, the Kerala Soil Museum and the Koyikkal Palace Museum. Agasthyamala Biosphere Reserve is listed in UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves.[141]
Cultureedit  
Main article: Culture of Thiruvananthapuram  
Established in 1855, the Napier Museum contains a vast collection of Ancient paintings and archaeological artefacts
Thiruvananthapuram is known as the "Evergreen City of India" because of its green landscapes and the presence of many public parks.[142] Thiruvananthapuram has historically been a cultural hub in Southern India due to the development of arts, architecture and liberal customs by the rulers of erstwhile Thiruvananthapuram. As a testimony to this, renowned artists like Maharaja Swathi Thirunal and Raja Ravi Varma hail from the city.[143][144] Prominent social reformers such as Sri Narayana Guru, Chattampi Swamikal, Ayyankali, Vakkom Moulavi and C. V. Raman Pillai also are from Thiruvananthapuram.[145]

Two of the three Malayalam triumvirate poets, Ulloor S. Parameswara Iyer and Kumaran Asan are from Thiruvananthapuram.[146][147] Annual literature festivals like the Kovalam Literary Festival, are held in the city.[148] Literary development is further aided by state institutions such as the State Central Library, one of the oldest public libraries in India, which was established in 1829,[149] and other major libraries including the Thiruvananthapuram Corporation Central library, and the Kerala University Library.[150] Thiruvananthapuram has been a hub of classical music since the days of Maharaja of Travancore, Swathi Thirunal.[151][152] Thiruvananthapuram is known for many music festivals like the Navarathri Music Festival, one of the oldest festivals of its kind in South India,[151] Swathi Sangeethotsavam, Soorya Music fest, Neelakanta Sivan Music Fest and many other music festivals are organised by various cultural groups.[151] The 111-day-long Soorya Festival is the biggest art and cultural event in Kerala.[153][154] The Soorya Festival features film festivals, theatre festivals, dance, music, painting and photography exhibitions.[153]

**Raja Ravi Varma** (Malayalam:[[ɾaːd͡ʒaː ɾɐʋi ʋɐrmːɐ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Malayalam "Help:IPA/Malayalam")) (29 April 1848 – 2 October 1906[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-4)) was an Indian painter. His works are one of the best examples of the fusion of European [academic art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_art "Academic art") with a purely Indian sensibility and iconography. He greatly enhanced his reach and influence as a painter and public figure by making affordable [lithographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithography "Lithography") of his paintings available to the public. His lithographs increased the involvement of common people with fine arts and defined artistic tastes. His religious depictions of Hindu deities and works from [Indian epic poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_epic_poetry "Indian epic poetry") and [Puranas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puranas "Puranas") have received critical acclaim. He was part of the royal family of [Parappanad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parappanad "Parappanad"), [Malappuram district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malappuram_district "Malappuram district").

Later in his life, two of his granddaughters were adopted into the royal family.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-5)

Varma was born on 29 April 1848, as [M. R. Ry.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maha_Raja_Rajya_Shri "Maha Raja Rajya Shri") Ravi Varma ([Malayalam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayalam_language "Malayalam language"): രവി വർമ്മ), [Koil Thampuran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koyi_Thampuran "Koyi Thampuran") of Kilimanoor at [Kilimanoor palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor_palace "Kilimanoor palace") in the erstwhile [princely state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princely_state "Princely state") of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore") (present-day [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala"))[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-pal-6) into an aristocratic family that for over 200 years produced consorts for the princesses of the matrilineal Travancore royal family. The title [Raja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja "Raja") was conferred as a personal title by the Viceroy and Governor-General of India [Lord Curzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Curzon "Lord Curzon").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-pal-6)
